title: Midwives exemptions, PGDs and controlled drugs
blurb: Know which medicines midwives and student midwives may give under the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 Schedule 17, when a PGD or prescription is needed, and how controlled drugs are handled.
question: Sam, a student midwife, is asked by his supervising midwife to give pethidine IM to Ella, who is in labour on a midwife-led unit. Is this lawful, and who may give it?

teach.h: Four lawful routes to give a prescription-only medicine
teach.body: A prescription-only medicine (POM) may be given under a prescription, a patient specific direction (PSD), a patient group direction (PGD) or an exemption in the law (RPS/RCN 2019). Formally, the midwives exemptions in Schedule 17 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 allow registered midwives to supply and administer specified POMs in the course of their professional practice without a prescription. In plain English: the law lists the core labour and newborn medicines a midwife can give on her own professional judgement.

Medicines

teach.h: Controlled drugs in maternity (NICE NG46; MDR 2001)
head: Rule
Detail
rows: Separate CD register (NG46 1.2.1); kept 2 years from last entry
Patient, date, time, drug, form, strength, dose, who gave it, any witness (1.7.4)
Record amount disposed of, signed by person and witness (1.7.8)
Tell the woman the name and dose (1.7.2)
teach.caption: Destruction of Schedule 2 stock needs an authorised witness (NG46 1.8.3). Most trusts also require a second person to witness each CD administration.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Sam and the pethidine
teach.body: Pethidine is on the Schedule 17 administration list, so the registered midwife can give it to Ella without a prescription, in her professional practice. But Sam is a student midwife: students may give listed medicines only under the direct supervision of a registered midwife, and never diamorphine, morphine or pethidine. So the registered midwife gives the pethidine herself, records it in the notes and the CD register with a witness, and Sam observes. Sam could give oxytocin for the third stage under direct supervision.

teach.text: Do not assume a medicine used every day in labour is on the list. Tranexamic acid and magnesium sulfate are standard obstetric drugs but are NOT midwives exemptions: they need a prescription or a PGD. And 'under supervision' does not let a student midwife give pethidine, diamorphine or morphine.

items: Routes: prescription, PSD, PGD or exemption (HMR 2012 Sch 17).
Midwives may administer listed parenteral POMs (oxytocins, ergometrine, carboprost, opioids, vitamin K, anti-D, fluids).
Lidocaine only while attending a woman in childbirth.
Students: direct supervision, and never pethidine, diamorphine or morphine.
PGD: defined group, named authorised staff, signed by doctor or dentist plus pharmacist, max 3 years.
Schedule 2 CDs: register, record each dose, record and witness part-ampoule disposal.

summary: You can now name the medicines midwives may supply and administer under Schedule 17, apply the limits for student midwives and lidocaine, and decide when a PGD or prescription is needed instead. You can also handle and record Schedule 2 controlled drugs such as pethidine safely.

A.q: A registered midwife on a birth centre needs to give a medicine without a prescription or PGD. Which can she administer under the Schedule 17 midwives exemptions?
options: Tranexamic acid IV
Magnesium sulfate IV
Carboprost IM
Gentamicin IV
A.why: Carboprost is on the HMR 2012 Schedule 17 list of parenteral POMs that registered midwives may administer.

whyNot.0: Tranexamic acid is not on the midwives list; it needs a prescription or PGD.
whyNot.1: Magnesium sulfate is not a midwives exemption medicine.
whyNot.3: Antibiotics such as gentamicin are not on the midwives list.

A.q: Under the direct supervision of a registered midwife, which medicine may a student midwife administer?
options: Pethidine IM for labour pain
Diamorphine IM for labour pain
Morphine IM for pain after the birth
Oxytocin IM for the third stage
A.why: Student midwives may administer Schedule 17 medicines under the direct supervision of a registered midwife, except diamorphine, morphine and pethidine.

whyNot.0: Pethidine is specifically excluded for student midwives.
whyNot.1: Diamorphine is specifically excluded for student midwives.
whyNot.2: Morphine is specifically excluded for student midwives.

A.q: Under Schedule 17, when may a registered midwife administer lidocaine without a prescription?
options: While attending a woman in childbirth
For any procedure on the postnatal ward
Before cannulation on the antenatal ward
For a newborn heel-prick blood test
A.why: Schedule 17 restricts lidocaine to administration while attending a woman in childbirth.

whyNot.1: The exemption does not extend to postnatal ward procedures in general.
whyNot.2: Antenatal cannulation is not attending a woman in childbirth.
whyNot.3: The exemption is for the woman in childbirth, not newborn procedures.

B.q: A student asks what a patient group direction is. Which answer is correct?
options: A prescriber's instruction for one named patient
A written instruction for a defined patient group
The list of medicines midwives may give by law
A verbal order confirmed in writing within 24 hours
B.why: A PGD is a written instruction allowing named, authorised registered professionals to supply or administer specified medicines to a defined group of patients without an individual prescription (MHRA).

whyNot.0: An instruction for one named patient is a prescription or patient specific direction.
whyNot.2: The legal list of midwives medicines is the Schedule 17 exemption, not a PGD.
whyNot.3: Verbal orders are a separate, exceptional route and are not PGDs.

B.q: A maternity unit is writing a new PGD. Which statement about PGDs is correct?
options: A nursing associate may work under it
It may run for up to 5 years
It cannot cover unlicensed medicines
Two midwives sign it to authorise it
B.why: MHRA: PGDs cannot be used for unlicensed medicines; they last a maximum of 3 years and are signed by a doctor or dentist plus a pharmacist.

whyNot.0: Nursing associates are not an eligible profession to use PGDs.
whyNot.1: The maximum period before expiry is 3 years.
whyNot.3: A doctor or dentist and a pharmacist sign the PGD.

B.q: A midwife needs 50 mg of pethidine and draws it from a 100 mg ampoule. What should happen to the remaining 50 mg?
options: Kept in the syringe for the next dose
Returned to the CD cupboard
Put in a sharps bin without a separate record
Disposal recorded, signed and witnessed
B.why: NICE NG46: record any leftover amount disposed of, with signatures of the person disposing and a witness.

whyNot.0: Keeping drawn-up opioid for later is unsafe and unaccountable.
whyNot.1: Opened ampoules cannot be returned to stock.
whyNot.2: Disposal of a controlled drug must be recorded and witnessed.

C.q: Tom, a student midwife, is directly supervised by a registered midwife. Straight after the birth he is about to infiltrate lidocaine before repairing a second-degree tear. Is this lawful?
options: Yes: lidocaine in childbirth, directly supervised
No: student midwives are excluded from lidocaine
Yes, but a prescription must be written first
No: student midwives need a signed PGD for lidocaine
C.why: Lidocaine is on the Schedule 17 list for administration while attending a woman in childbirth, and students may administer listed medicines (other than the three opioids) under the direct supervision of a registered midwife.

whyNot.1: The student exclusion covers diamorphine, morphine and pethidine, not lidocaine.
whyNot.2: No prescription is needed: the exemption covers this.
whyNot.3: Students cannot be authorised to work under PGDs; the exemption applies here.

C.q: A midwife is asked to give a medicine covered by the ward's PGD, but she has not been assessed and authorised to use that PGD. What should she do?
options: Give it, as the PGD covers all ward midwives
Give it under her own Schedule 17 midwives exemption
Use another lawful route, such as a prescription
Give it and ask an authorised colleague to sign
C.why: Only named, authorised professionals may work under a PGD, so she needs another lawful route, such as an individual prescription (MHRA; Code 18).

whyNot.0: A PGD applies to named, authorised individuals, not every midwife on the ward.
whyNot.1: A medicine covered by a PGD is not necessarily on the Schedule 17 list.
whyNot.3: Another person's signature cannot make an unauthorised administration lawful.

C.q: A community midwife visits a breastfeeding mother whose baby has oral thrush. Which medicine could she supply under the HMR 2012 exemptions in her professional practice?
options: Flucloxacillin
Codeine
Nystatin
Enoxaparin
C.why: Nystatin (and miconazole) is on the Schedule 17 list of POMs that registered midwives may supply in the course of their professional practice.

whyNot.0: Antibiotics are not on the midwives supply list.
whyNot.1: Codeine is not on the midwives list and is not used in breastfeeding (SPS).
whyNot.3: LMWH such as enoxaparin needs a prescription or PGD.

reteach.title: The midwife's legal toolkit
reteach.question: Think of the medicines in a midwife's bag at a home birth. Why can she give them without a doctor?

blocks.h: The law did the prescribing in advance
blocks.body: Parliament wrote a list into Schedule 17 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012: the medicines a midwife needs to keep a woman and baby safe in normal birth and its common emergencies. Oxytocin and ergometrine for bleeding, opioids and naloxone, vitamin K, anti-D, fluids, adrenaline. Anything not on the list, such as tranexamic acid, needs a prescription or a PGD, however routine it feels.

blocks.text: Direct supervision widens what a student may do for most listed medicines, but it never covers the three opioids: pethidine, diamorphine and morphine.

explain.body: Registered midwives may administer the Schedule 17 parenteral POMs (and supply the supply-list items) in the course of their professional practice, without a prescription or PGD.

test.q: A midwife gives oxytocin 10 units IM for the third stage with no prescription. Which legal route allows this?
options: A patient specific direction
The midwives exemptions in HMR 2012
A verbal order from the obstetrician
Standard 18 of the NMC Code
test.why: Oxytocins are on the Schedule 17 list that registered midwives may administer in their professional practice.

whyNot.0: A PSD is a prescriber's written instruction for a named patient, not needed here.
whyNot.2: No verbal order is needed for a listed medicine.
whyNot.3: The Code sets professional standards; it is not a legal authority to give POMs.

explain.body: Students may administer Schedule 17 medicines only under the direct supervision of a registered midwife, and the exemption does not include diamorphine, morphine or pethidine for them.

test.q: Under Schedule 17, which medicine is a student midwife excluded from administering, even under supervision?
options: Oxytocin
Phytomenadione
Morphine
Anti-D immunoglobulin
test.why: Schedule 17 excludes diamorphine, morphine and pethidine from student midwife administration.

whyNot.0: Oxytocin may be given by a student under direct supervision.
whyNot.1: Vitamin K may be given by a student under direct supervision.
whyNot.3: Anti-D may be given by a student under direct supervision.

explain.body: A PGD lets named, authorised registered professionals supply or administer a specified medicine to a defined group. It is signed by a doctor or dentist plus a pharmacist, expires after a maximum of 3 years and cannot cover unlicensed medicines (MHRA).

test.q: Who must sign a patient group direction?
options: Two registered midwives
A doctor or dentist and a pharmacist
The ward manager and a midwife
A pharmacist and a nursing associate
test.why: MHRA: a PGD is signed by a doctor or dentist and a pharmacist (plus organisational authorisation).

whyNot.0: Midwives may use PGDs but do not authorise them as the clinical signatories.
whyNot.2: A ward manager is not one of the required clinical signatories.
whyNot.3: Nursing associates are not eligible to use PGDs, let alone sign them.

explain.body: Pethidine, diamorphine and morphine are Schedule 2 controlled drugs. Keep a CD register, record each administration (including any witness), record and witness disposal of part ampoules, and destroy Schedule 2 stock only in front of an authorised witness (NG46 1.2.1, 1.7.4, 1.7.8, 1.8.3).

test.q: In which schedule of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001 is pethidine?
options: Schedule 3
Schedule 4
Schedule 5
Schedule 2
test.why: Pethidine, like diamorphine and morphine, is a Schedule 2 controlled drug, needing a CD register and witnessed records.

whyNot.1: Schedule 4 Part 1 includes benzodiazepines such as diazepam.
whyNot.2: Schedule 5 covers low-strength preparations such as some codeine products.
